title: Part 2, Chapter 59
paragraphs: Which relates the strange thing, one that might well be called an adventure, that befell Don Quixote

A clear, fresh spring they came upon in a cool grove washed away the dust and weariness that the bulls’ rude treatment had left on Don Quixote and Sancho, and beside it, after turning Dapple and Rocinante loose without halter or bridle, the dejected pair, master and servant, sat down. Sancho went to the storehouse of his saddlebags and brought out of them what he liked to call the grub; Don Quixote rinsed his mouth and bathed his face, and the cool water revived his drooping spirits. Out of sheer vexation he ate nothing, and out of sheer courtesy Sancho did not dare touch a bite of what lay before him, but waited for his master to taste it first. Seeing, though, that Don Quixote, lost in his thoughts, was forgetting to lift the bread to his lips, he said not a word, and, trampling every rule of good manners underfoot, began packing into his belly whatever bread and cheese came to hand.

“Eat, Sancho my friend,” said Don Quixote; “sustain your life, which matters more to you than mine does to me, and leave me to die under the weight of my thoughts and the press of my misfortunes. I was born, Sancho, to live dying, and you to die eating; and to see how true this is, consider me: printed in histories, famous in arms, courteous in conduct, honored by princes, courted by maidens — and yet, just when I was looking forward to the palms, triumphs, and crowns that my valiant deeds had won and earned, I found myself this very morning trodden down, kicked, and pounded under the hooves of filthy, unclean beasts. The thought of it dulls my teeth, numbs my jaws, cripples my hands, and strips me of all appetite for food — so much so that I have half a mind to let myself die of hunger, the cruelest of all deaths.”

“So then,” said Sancho, chewing busily all the while, “your worship doesn’t hold with the proverb that says, ‘Let Martha die, so long as she dies with a full belly.’ I, at any rate, have no intention of killing myself; far from it — I mean to do what the cobbler does, who stretches the leather with his teeth until it reaches as far as he needs. I’ll stretch my life out by eating until it reaches the end heaven has set for it; and let me tell you, señor, there’s no greater madness than wanting to die of despair, the way your worship does. Take my advice: after you’ve eaten, lie down and sleep a while on this green mattress of grass, and you’ll find that when you wake you’ll feel a good deal better.”

Don Quixote did as he suggested, for Sancho’s reasoning struck him as more a philosopher’s than a fool’s, and he said, “Sancho, if you would do for me what I am about to ask, my relief would be more certain and my heaviness of heart not so great. It is this: while I sleep, following your advice, go off a little way, bare your flesh to the open air, and give yourself three or four hundred lashes with Rocinante’s reins, on account of the three thousand and some you are bound to give yourself for Dulcinea’s disenchantment; for it is a great pity that the poor lady should remain enchanted through your carelessness and neglect.”

“There’s a good deal to be said about that,” said Sancho; “for now let’s both get some sleep, and after that, God has already decreed what will happen. Your worship should know that whipping oneself in cold blood is a hard business, especially when the lashes land on a body that’s badly nourished and worse fed. Let my lady Dulcinea be patient; when she’s least expecting it she’ll see me whipped till I look like a sieve, and ‘until death it’s all life’ — I mean, I still have life in me, along with the will to make good what I’ve promised.”

Don Quixote thanked him, ate a little, and Sancho ate a great deal, and then the two of them lay down to sleep, leaving those inseparable friends and companions, Rocinante and Dapple, to their own devices, free to graze at will on the plentiful grass the meadow offered. They woke fairly late, mounted again, and continued on their way, pressing forward to reach an inn that appeared to be about a league off. I say an inn, because Don Quixote called it one, against his usual habit of calling every inn a castle. When they arrived, they asked the landlord whether they could lodge there. He said yes, and with all the comfort and good fare they could find in Saragossa. They dismounted, and Sancho stowed his provisions in a room to which the landlord gave him the key. He led the animals to the stable, gave them their feed, and came back to see what orders Don Quixote — who was seated on a bench by the door — might have for him, offering particular thanks to heaven that his master had not taken this inn for a castle. Supper-time came; they withdrew to their room, and Sancho asked the landlord what he had to give them for supper. The landlord replied that his mouth should be the measure: he had only to ask for whatever he liked, since that inn was stocked with the birds of the air, the fowls of the earth, and the fish of the sea.
“No need for all that,” said Sancho; “if they’ll roast us a couple of chickens we’ll be content, for my master is delicate and eats little, and I’m not excessively greedy myself.”
The landlord answered that he had no chickens, because the kites had carried them off.
“In that case,” said Sancho, “let señor landlord have a pullet roasted, and see that it’s a tender one.”
“A pullet! By my father!” said the landlord; “the honest truth is that only yesterday I sent more than fifty off to the city to sell. But apart from pullets, ask for anything you please.”
“Then surely,” said Sancho, “you won’t be short of veal or kid.”
“Just at the moment,” said the landlord, “there’s none in the house, because it’s all run out; but next week there will be more than enough.”
“A lot of good that does us,” said Sancho; “I’d lay a bet that all these shortages are going to end up amounting to plenty of bacon and eggs.”

“By God,” said the landlord, “my guest must be slow-witted indeed; I tell him I have neither pullets nor hens, and he wants me to have eggs! Run through some other delicacies, if you please, and stop asking about anything in the way of poultry.”
“Body of me!” said Sancho, “let’s settle this: tell me once and for all what you do have, and let’s waste no more words on it.”

“What I truly and honestly have, señor guest,” said the landlord, “is a pair of cow-heels that look like calves’ feet, or a pair of calves’ feet that look like cow-heels; they’re stewed with chickpeas, onions, and bacon, and at this very moment they’re calling out, ‘Come and eat me, come and eat me.’”

“I claim them as mine here and now,” said Sancho; “let no one lay a hand on them. I’ll pay better for them than anyone else would, because nothing could suit my taste more, and it doesn’t matter a pin to me whether they’re feet or heels.”
“No one shall touch them,” said the landlord; “for the other guests I have, being people of high rank, travel with their own cook, caterer, and larder.”

“If it’s a question of rank,” said Sancho, “nobody outranks my master; but the calling he follows allows for no larders or pantries. We simply stretch ourselves out in the middle of a meadow and fill up on acorns or medlars.”

There the conversation between Sancho and the landlord ended, Sancho having no wish to carry it further by answering him; for the landlord had already asked him what calling or what profession it was his master followed.

When supper-time came, then, Don Quixote retired to his room, the landlord brought in the stew-pot just as it was, and he sat down to eat with great determination. It seems that in another room, next to Don Quixote’s and separated from it by nothing more than a thin partition, he overheard these words: “On your life, Señor Don Jeronimo, while supper is being brought, let us read another chapter of the Second Part of ‘Don Quixote of La Mancha.’”

The instant Don Quixote heard his own name he sprang to his feet and listened with sharpened ears to catch what they were saying about him, and he heard the Don Jeronimo who had been addressed reply, “Why would you have us read such nonsense, Don Juan, when no one who has read the First Part of the history of ‘Don Quixote of La Mancha’ can possibly take any pleasure in reading this Second Part?”

“Even so,” said the one called Don Juan, “we would do well to read it, since there is no book so bad that it doesn’t contain something good. What displeases me most about this one is that it portrays Don Quixote as cured by now of his love for Dulcinea del Toboso.”

At this Don Quixote, full of rage and indignation, raised his voice and said, “Whoever says that Don Quixote of La Mancha has forgotten, or could ever forget, Dulcinea del Toboso, I will teach him with equal arms how far he stands from the truth; for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso cannot be forgotten, nor can forgetfulness find any room in Don Quixote. Constancy is his motto, and his profession is to uphold it with his life and never betray it.”
“Who is it that answers us?” said those in the next room.
“Who should it be,” said Sancho, “but Don Quixote of La Mancha himself, who will stand behind everything he has said and everything he has yet to say? A good payer isn’t troubled by his pledges.”

Sancho had hardly spoken these words when two gentlemen — for such they appeared to be — came into the room, and one of them, throwing his arms around Don Quixote’s neck, said to him, “Your appearance leaves no doubt about your name, nor can your name fail to vouch for your appearance: beyond question, señor, you are the true Don Quixote of La Mancha, north star and morning light of knight-errantry, in spite and in defiance of the man who has tried to usurp your name and wipe out your achievements, as the author of this book I here present to you has done.” With that he placed a book his companion was carrying into Don Quixote’s hands; Don Quixote took it and, without a word, began running his eye over it, but shortly handed it back, saying, “In the little I have seen, I have found three things in this author that deserve censure. The first is certain words I have read in the preface; the second, that the language is Aragonese, since he sometimes writes without articles; and the third — the one that above all convicts him of ignorance — is that he blunders and strays from the truth in the most essential point of the history, for here he says that the wife of my squire Sancho Panza is named Mari Gutierrez, when she is called no such thing, but Teresa Panza; and when a man gets so important a point wrong, there is good reason to fear he is wrong about every other point in the history.”

“A fine sort of historian, to be sure!” cried Sancho at this; “he must know a great deal about our affairs, if he calls my wife Teresa Panza Mari Gutierrez. Take the book back, señor, and see whether I’m in it and whether he’s changed my name too.”
“From the way you talk, friend,” said Don Jeronimo, “you must surely be Sancho Panza, Señor Don Quixote’s squire.”
“I am,” said Sancho; “and proud of it.”

“Well then, by my faith,” said the gentleman, “this new author doesn’t treat you with the decency your person displays. He makes you out a gross feeder and a simpleton, not in the least amusing — a very different creature from the Sancho described in the First Part of your master’s history.”
“God forgive him,” said Sancho; “he could have left me in my corner without troubling his head about me at all. ‘Let him who knows how, ring the bells’; ‘Saint Peter is well off in Rome.’”

The two gentlemen urged Don Quixote to come to their room and share their supper, for they knew very well there was nothing in that inn fit for a man of his quality. Don Quixote, courteous as ever, yielded to their invitation and supped with them. Sancho stayed behind with the stew, and, vested with full delegated authority, seated himself at the head of the table, with the landlord beside him, who was every bit as devoted to cow-heels and calves’ feet as Sancho was.

Over supper Don Juan asked Don Quixote what news he had of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso: was she married, had she given birth, was she with child, or did she remain a maiden — keeping her modesty and delicacy intact — and still cherish the memory of Señor Don Quixote’s tender devotion?

To this he replied, “Dulcinea is a maiden still, my passion more deeply rooted than ever, our dealings as unrewarding as before, and her beauty transformed into that of a coarse peasant girl.” Then he went on to give them a full and detailed account of Dulcinea’s enchantment, of what had befallen him in the cave of Montesinos, and of the remedy the sage Merlin had prescribed for her disenchantment — namely, the whipping of Sancho.

The two gentlemen took the greatest delight in hearing Don Quixote relate the strange events of his history, and they were as much astonished by his absurdities as by the elegant style in which he delivered them. At one moment they took him for a man of intelligence and good sense; at the next he seemed to them a rambling fool; and they could not settle where, between wisdom and folly, they ought to place him.

Sancho, having finished his supper and left the landlord laid out in the shape of an X, went off to the room where his master was, and as he came in he said, “Strike me dead, sirs, if the author of that book your worships have there wants the two of us to stay on good terms. Since he calls me a glutton — according to what your worships say — I only hope he doesn’t call me a drunkard as well.”

“He does call you that,” said Don Jeronimo; “though I can’t recall just how he puts it. I know only that his words are offensive, and lies besides, as I can see plainly enough from the face of the worthy Sancho here before me.”

“Take my word for it,” said Sancho, “the Sancho and the Don Quixote in that history must be different people from the ones who appear in the history Cide Hamete Benengeli wrote — which is to say, ourselves: my master valiant, wise, and true in love; and I simple and droll, and neither a glutton nor a drunkard.”

“I believe it,” said Don Juan; “and if it were possible, an order ought to be issued that no one presume to deal with anything concerning Don Quixote except Cide Hamete, his original author — just as Alexander commanded that no one presume to paint his portrait but Apelles.”
“Let anyone who pleases paint me,” said Don Quixote, “but let him not mistreat me; for patience will often give way when insults are heaped upon it.”

“No insult can be offered to Señor Don Quixote,” said Don Juan, “that he is not able to avenge — unless he turns it aside with the shield of his patience, which, by my reckoning, is great and strong.”

A good part of the night went by in talk of this kind, and though Don Juan wanted Don Quixote to read more of the book and see how it went on, he could not be persuaded. He said that he considered it read, pronounced the whole of it foolish, and added that if it should somehow reach the author’s ears that he had held it in his hands, he did not want the man flattering himself that Don Quixote had actually read it; for our thoughts — and our eyes still more — should keep their distance from whatever is obscene and foul.

They asked him where he intended to go next. He answered, to Saragossa, to take part in the jousts in armor that were held in that city every year. Don Juan told him that the new history related how Don Quixote — whoever this Don Quixote might be — had competed there in a tilting at the ring, in a contest barren of invention, threadbare in its mottoes, beggarly in its costumes, though rich in stupidities.

“For that very reason,” said Don Quixote, “I will not set foot in Saragossa; and in that way I will expose this new historian’s lie to the whole world, and people will see that I am not the Don Quixote he writes about.”
“That is the wise course,” said Don Jeronimo; “and there are other jousts at Barcelona, where Señor Don Quixote may display his valor.”
“So I intend,” said Don Quixote; “and since it is now time, I beg your worships to give me leave to retire to bed, and to count and keep me among the number of your truest friends and servants.”
“Me too,” said Sancho; “I may turn out to be good for something.”

With that they said their farewells, and Don Quixote and Sancho withdrew to their room, leaving Don Juan and Don Jeronimo marveling at the mixture he made of good sense and madness, and fully convinced that these two, and not the pair their Aragonese author had described, were the genuine Don Quixote and Sancho. Don Quixote rose early, and took leave of his hosts by rapping on the partition of the other room. Sancho paid the landlord handsomely, and advised him either to promise less about the provisions of his inn or to keep it better provided.
